topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: 15 U.S.C. 1, Section 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act, declares illegal:
choice_a: Every contract, combination, or conspiracy in restraint of trade or commerce among the states
choice_b: Any single firm's unilateral decision to raise its own prices
choice_c: Any merger between two real estate brokerages
choice_d: Any advertisement of a commission rate
explanation: 15 U.S.C. 1 declares illegal every contract, combination, or conspiracy in restraint of trade or commerce among the states -- the foundational antitrust prohibition applied to real estate brokerage conduct.

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: Two competing brokerage firms secretly agree that both will charge clients a flat 6% commission rate. This conduct is:
choice_a: Legal, as long as clients are told the rate is non-negotiable
choice_b: A per se violation of Sherman Act Section 1's price-fixing prohibition
choice_c: Legal, since 6% is a common industry rate
choice_d: Only illegal if a third firm joins the agreement
explanation: An agreement between competing firms to fix commission rates is a classic per se violation of Sherman Act Section 1 -- each firm must set its own commission rates independently, and rates must remain negotiable.

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: A group of brokers agrees among themselves to refuse to show properties listed by a discount or limited-service brokerage. This is an example of:
choice_c: A group boycott, a per se violation of Sherman Act Section 1
explanation: An agreement among competing firms to refuse to deal with a particular firm or type of business, such as a discount brokerage, is a group boycott and a per se violation of Sherman Act Section 1.

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: Two competing brokerage firms agree that Firm A will only take listings north of Main Street and Firm B will only take listings south of Main Street. This is an example of:
choice_d: Market allocation, a per se violation of Sherman Act Section 1
explanation: Agreements between competitors to divide up territories, price ranges, or customer types so they don't compete for the same business are market-allocation agreements and a per se violation of Sherman Act Section 1.

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: A listing firm tells a buyer that an offer will only be accepted if the buyer agrees to use the listing firm's in-house mortgage company. Conditioning one service on the purchase of a second, separate service like this is known as:
choice_a: A tying arrangement, which can raise antitrust concerns
explanation: Conditioning the provision of one service on the client's purchase of a separate service is a tying arrangement, which can violate antitrust law when the party imposing the condition has market power -- a concern that parallels Wisconsin's own tie-in-arrangement conduct rule.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. 1 (Sherman Act Section 1); Wis. Admin. Code REEB 24.075

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: Sherman Act Section 1 requires proof of a "conspiracy," meaning:
choice_a: Any single broker's business decision, made without input from a competitor
choice_b: An agreement or meeting of the minds between two or more separate, competing firms or persons
choice_c: Any agreement between a broker and the broker's own client
choice_d: Any decision made by a firm's managing broker
explanation: Sherman Act Section 1 requires concerted action -- an agreement or meeting of the minds between two or more separate, competing firms or persons; it does not reach a single firm's unilateral, independent business decisions.

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: A single real estate firm unilaterally decides, entirely on its own, to charge an unusually high commission rate. This decision:
choice_c: Does NOT violate Sherman Act Section 1, because Section 1 requires concerted action between two or more competitors, not unilateral action
choice_d: Must be lowered to match competitors under federal law
explanation: A firm's unilateral pricing decision, made without any agreement with a competitor, does not violate Sherman Act Section 1 -- even an unusually high rate is lawful unilateral conduct as long as it results from no agreement with another firm.

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: Two competing agents discuss commission rates, or which competitors to work with, at an MLS or board meeting -- even without reaching an explicit agreement. This kind of discussion:
choice_b: Only matters legally if a client later complains
choice_c: Cannot create any legal risk under federal law
choice_d: Can create a legal inference of an unlawful conspiracy, which is why licensees are trained to avoid such topics altogether with competitors
explanation: Even informal discussion of commission rates, fees, or which competitors to deal with can create a legal inference of price fixing or group boycott without an explicit agreement, so licensees are trained to avoid these topics with competitors entirely.
source_note: REEB 25.023(8)(c) -- situations creating inferences of price fixing/boycott

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: An individual convicted of a Sherman Act Section 1 violation faces which of the following potential penalties?
choice_a: A felony conviction, with a fine of up to $1,000,000 and/or up to 10 years' imprisonment
choice_b: A civil fine only, with no possibility of imprisonment
choice_c: License suspension by the Real Estate Examining Board only
choice_d: No penalty unless the conduct also independently violates state law
explanation: A Sherman Act Section 1 violation is a felony; an individual faces a fine of up to $1,000,000 and/or up to 10 years' imprisonment, while a corporation faces a fine of up to $100,000,000.

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: A real estate consumer injured by a price-fixing conspiracy among competing brokers may pursue a private civil remedy of:
choice_a: A refund of the commission only
choice_b: Treble (triple) damages under the Clayton Act's private right of action
choice_c: No remedy; only the federal government may sue
choice_d: A public apology from the offending firms
explanation: The Clayton Act gives private parties injured by a Sherman Act violation the right to sue for treble (triple) damages, in addition to any DOJ Antitrust Division or state attorney general enforcement action.
source_note: Clayton Act private right of action; 15 U.S.C. 1
